constraints.evidence: Slide 17: plan leaves $2.5M at month 18, 6.2 months against the 12-month floor; floor needs $4.8M. Also states that if the $9.5M excludes core burn, $7.2M more goes and cash runs out first. Slide 22: $14.3M needed vs $12.0M in the bank.

Condition 3 (slide 22) requires funding 'without a new round'. Slide 21 compares software ($0.8M a year, 'no new funding round') with $9.5M for launch. Slide 18 notes losses are 'before launch marketing and head-office costs'. It never says that contribution-positive is not company profitability.

Slides 8-11: full stack built from Table 3. Contribution per order is +$2.02 plan, -$1.76 best inputs, -$6.17 median, -$12.57 pop-up. Median rider cost $7.40 and store $3.50. The best-inputs case is flagged as a combination no site achieved. The break-even order value is about $47 before store costs and about $63 with them.

Slides 9, 13: pop-up at $31 AOV, 2.1 orders/rider-hour, 280 orders/day, 12% promotions, -$12.57 per order. Promotions 'bought the 18% weekly growth'. The document does not give the implied final-week rate (~410/day).

Slide 15: $38 / 22% = $172.7 per retained customer; payback 14.8 months at the plan's pre-store $3.77, about 28 months after store costs, never at benchmark or pop-up economics. Slide 14 separates the 44% stated intent from observed behaviour (0.7 orders a week). It does not size the customers needed to fill a store.

Slide 11 and condition 2 (slide 22): 2 of 3 cities are considering minimum pay, which 'can only push this line up'. Rider cost is shown as the largest cost line. The document does not quantify the effect of a $1/hour rise on any case or show any headroom after a pay increase.

Slides 4-5: GMV grew 2.8x with yearly growth of 44%, 38% and 42%. Zipcart is at -$1.90 per order and -25.8% EBITDA margin; QuickBasket at -$3.40 and -45.7%, closing 4 of 11 cities. 'Demand is not the question' states that growth is not evidence of profit.

Slide 6 gives the $3.99 fee, promotions cut to 1%, -14% volume and +$0.40 in the densest city, and calls it the most favourable case. The document never applies this pricing to Parcelbird's inputs (no +$2.25 at best density, no -$0.48 at median, no break-even density). It says only that 'our plan charges only the $1.99 delivery fee, so it cannot copy the route'.

Slide 21: $0.8M / ($96k x 81%) = 10.3 contracts; the 9 late-stage deals give about $0.9M ARR and cover 87% of the hiring cost; runway goes from 30 to 26 months with no new contract. The $5.6M floor is not stated, and the document does not show software break-even within current cash.

alternatives.evidence: Adopted as the recommendation. Slide 21 and slide 20 give the 10.3-contract break-even, late-stage pipeline of $0.9M ARR, runway 30 to 26 months, and grocer demand for fast delivery from existing stores. It is compared against the other two options on the board's criteria. There is no conversion-rate evidence and no demonstrated break-even within current cash.

No capped, capital-light, fee-priced test run from a grocer partner's store, with cash cap and kill criteria, is evaluated. 'Package fast delivery from existing stores as a software offer' is a product offer to grocers, not a Parcelbird-run test.

Slide 20 and the Alternatives section: 'Test one permanent dark store first: Not now'. One store at median economics loses about $2.0M a year (328,500 x -$6.17), taking runway below 12 months within about 8 months. It assumes 900 orders/day from day one, not the pop-up's 280, and does not test a fee or AOV-based stage gate.

Slides 8-10, 17-18: every plan input exceeds the best observed site, the plan leaves 6.2 months of runway, and nine median stores lose about $18M a year. The upside is acknowledged: about +$12M a year at plan inputs. The fee route is only partly addressed (slide 6).

sensitivities.evidence: Slides 8-10: contribution per order at four input sets (+$2.02, -$1.76, -$6.17, -$12.57). Break-even order value is $46.7 before store costs and about $63 with store costs at 900/day. The median order loses $2.67 before store cost, so volume alone cannot fix it. Slide 11 shows rider cost falling from $7.40 to $5.92 at 3.0 orders/hour. The effect of a rider-pay increase per $1/hour is not quantified, and the break-even AOV at best density (~$50) is not given.

Zipcart's fee, promotions cut and -14% volume are named on slide 6, and slide 13 shows promotions at 12% vs 6%. There is no calculation of Parcelbird's contribution at a $3.99 fee and 1% promotions, no break-even density under that pricing, and no volume-loss tolerance. Slide 14 notes retention may fall once promotions are cut.

Slide 17: $2.5M and 6.2 months left vs 12 required, plus the $7.2M extra if the burn is excluded. Slide 22: $14.3M needed, $2.3M short. Slide 20: one store breaches 12 months in about 8 months. Slide 21: software costs $0.8M a year, runway 30 to 26 months. Slide 18: nine median stores lose $18M a year, 1.5x cash. The maximum spend that keeps 12 months (~$7.2M, ~$6.4M after hires) is not stated as a sizing ceiling.

overclaim.quote: Promotions explain almost half of the pop-up's extra loss per order

omissions: The 'almost half' (47.4%) holds only for loss before store costs. Including the temporary store ($6.36 vs $3.50 at median), the extra loss is about $6.40 per order and promotions are $1.68, about 26%. The summary line drops that scope; the governing thought itself (do not launch) is not overclaimed.

No fee-priced scenario at Parcelbird's own inputs. The document says the plan 'cannot copy' Zipcart's route, yet a $3.99 fee is a choice the company could make. The board lacks the +$2.25 (best density) / -$0.48 (median) result and the break-even density of roughly 700-1,040 orders/day, which is the founders' strongest rebuttal.
No capped, partner-store test with kill criteria (A2). The only alternatives to the full plan are a permanent own-store test and the software path.
The software recommendation is not shown to reach profitability within current cash. It uses no conversion rates, and the 12-month floor after the hires (~$5.6M) is not stated.
Rider-pay headroom is not quantified (about $0.29-0.42 per order per $1/hour), so the board cannot see how sensitive any future revisit case is.
The document states no maximum new-spend ceiling (~$7.2M, falling with burn) against which a staged test could be sized, and no wind-down cash scenario if a test fails.
unsupported_assumptions: "About 10 new contracts pay for the $0.8M a year of hires" assumes every contract is incremental to the hires, at the $96k average and 81% gross margin. The document admits 'the pack gives no conversion rates'.
"Positive margin from the first contract" assumes no onboarding or support cost beyond the 81% gross margin.
"Our plan charges only the $1.99 delivery fee, so it cannot copy the route to profit that Zipcart took" assumes pricing is fixed. Nothing in the pack says so.
"As an operator we would become their competitor" and "competes with our customers" rest on no evidence of how pipeline grocers would react.
The one-store test ("loses about $2.0M a year", below 12 months within about 8 months) assumes median density of 900 orders/day from day one. The pop-up averaged 280, so this is generous to the test.
